subject: Geography
name: Geography, Year 7
about: Australian Curriculum, Year 7: Water in the world, Place and liveability
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Place
points.brief: A place is a part of the Earth's surface that people give meaning to. Geographers describe what a place is like and why people value it differently.

points.title: Space
points.brief: Space is about where things are and how they are spread out. Geographers look at location, distance and the pattern something makes on a map.

points.title: Environment
points.brief: The environment is the living and non-living world around us. People depend on it and change it, and it shapes how people live.

points.title: Interconnection
points.brief: Nothing in geography stands alone. People, places and environments are linked, so a change in one place can affect another far away.

points.title: Sustainability
points.brief: Sustainability means using environments in ways that let them keep supporting people and other living things into the future.

points.title: Scale
points.brief: Geographers study things at local, regional, national and global scales, and the cause of something can look different at each scale.

points.title: Change
points.brief: Places and environments change over time, some quickly and some over centuries. Knowing why they changed helps predict what comes next.

points.title: Map conventions
points.brief: A good map has a border, orientation (a north arrow), a legend, a title, a scale and a source, often remembered as BOLTSS.

points.title: Latitude and longitude
points.brief: Lines of latitude run east to west and measure degrees north or south of the equator. Lines of longitude measure degrees east or west of the prime meridian.

points.title: Describing a distribution
points.brief: A distribution is how something is spread across space. Geographers describe it as clustered, scattered, linear or even, and say where it is most and least common.

points.title: Primary and secondary data
points.brief: Primary data is collected first-hand, such as a survey or fieldwork. Secondary data was collected by someone else, such as census figures or a report.

points.title: Renewable, non-renewable and continuous resources
points.brief: Renewable resources, such as forests, can replace themselves. Non-renewable ones, such as coal, run out. Continuous ones, such as sunlight and wind, never run out.

points.title: The water cycle
points.brief: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, then runs off over land or soaks into the ground and back to the sea.

points.title: Forms of water
points.brief: Most of Earth's water is salt water, and much of the fresh water is ice or groundwater. Water vapour, ice and salt water can all become a resource.

points.title: Green water and blue water
points.brief: Green water is the moisture held in soil that plants use. Blue water is the water in rivers, lakes, dams and underground that people can collect.

points.title: How moving water changes places
points.brief: Moving water links places, carrying water and soil downstream. It also erodes rock and soil, cutting valleys and shaping the land.

points.title: Where Australia's water is
points.brief: Australia is the driest inhabited continent. Rain falls most on the north and east coasts, and large stores of groundwater lie under the inland, such as the Great Artesian Basin.

points.title: Why water supply varies
points.brief: Climate, seasons, landforms and high evaporation make rainfall and river flow vary a lot from place to place and year to year in Australia.

points.title: Physical and economic water scarcity
points.brief: Physical scarcity is when there is not enough water. Economic scarcity is when water exists but people cannot reach it, because dams, pipes or money are lacking.

points.title: Competing uses of water
points.brief: Farms, towns, industry and rivers themselves all need water, so sharing it is hard, especially in dry years.

points.title: Managing water sustainably
points.brief: Ways to make water last include recycling grey water, harvesting stormwater, desalination, water trading and using less at home and on farms.

points.title: The economic value of water
points.brief: Water supports farms and towns. The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area in New South Wales and the Mekong Delta in Vietnam both grow rice with irrigation.

points.title: Water and First Nations Australians
points.brief: For First Nations Australians, rivers, waterholes, soaks and springs carry cultural and spiritual meaning and connect people to Country, as well as giving water and food.

points.title: Water's beauty and spiritual meaning
points.brief: People value water for its beauty, such as waterfalls and bays protected as national parks or World Heritage sites, and for its spiritual meaning, such as the Ganges for Hindus.

points.title: What makes a natural hazard
points.brief: A natural event becomes a hazard when it can harm people or property. Atmospheric hazards come from the weather, and hydrological hazards come from water.

points.title: Drought
points.brief: A drought is a long period of below-average rainfall. It dries out soil and dams, hurts farms and towns, and builds slowly over months or years.

points.title: Floods and tropical cyclones
points.brief: Floods happen when heavy rain overfills rivers or drains. Tropical cyclones form over warm seas and bring destructive winds, heavy rain and storm surges.

points.title: Prevention, mitigation and preparedness
points.brief: Prevention stops harm happening, mitigation reduces the harm, and preparedness gets people ready, such as levees, building rules and warning systems.

points.title: What liveability means
points.brief: Liveability is how well a place meets people's needs for a good life, such as safety, services, jobs, a clean environment and things to do.

points.title: Measuring liveability
points.brief: Objective measures count things, such as transport or hospitals. Subjective measures ask people how they feel about a place, so the same place can rate differently.

points.title: Environmental quality and where people live
points.brief: Clean air and water, green space, views and a pleasant climate draw people to a place, and pollution pushes them away.

points.title: Reasons people move to a place
points.brief: People choose where to live for work, family and culture, or a lifestyle change, such as a tree change to the country or a sea change to the coast.

points.title: Types of settlement
points.brief: Australian settlements range from urban cities to rural towns, remote and very remote communities, depending on their size and distance from services.

points.title: Access to services
points.brief: Hospitals, schools and shops cluster in cities, so people in remote places often travel far for them, which affects liveability.

points.title: Transport, technology and access
points.brief: Public transport, roads and the internet let people reach services and activities. Without them, a place is harder to live in.

points.title: Feeling safe and connected
points.brief: People rate a place as more liveable when they feel safe, included and connected to others there, and less when they feel left out or threatened.

points.title: Connection to Country
points.brief: First Nations Australians have deep connections to Country/Place through family, culture and history, including dispossession and relocation, which shape identity and belonging.

points.title: Strategies to improve liveability
points.brief: Councils make places more liveable with better public spaces, walking and cycling paths, transport links and waste and recycling services.

points.title: Liveability for everyone
points.brief: A liveable place works for young people, older people and people with disability, such as with ramps, parks for teenagers and good public transport.

points.title: Learning from Europe
points.brief: Cities such as Copenhagen built safe bike lanes and car-free streets, and Australian cities can judge whether those ideas would work locally.

points.title: Judging a liveability strategy
points.brief: To judge a strategy, set criteria such as cost, who benefits and its effect on the environment, then weigh the strategy against each one.
